source.title: Learning Multi-Level Features with Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Bart Bussmann; Noa Nabeshima; Adam Karvonen; Neel Nanda

record.tranche_reason: The study directly measures feature absorption and splitting, but uses nested-reconstruction SAEs and first-letter classification probes to test these effects.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports downstream probing, erasure, reconstruction, and interpretability results; those are not rows unless they measure feature absorption, splitting, or the cross-size feature relationships in the claim. The tree-matching threshold is a methodological choice, not a result.
record.test_reason: The study measures absorption and splitting directly: a toy hierarchical model, TinyStories reference SAEs of growing size, and first-letter absorption and splitting probes on Gemma-2-2B. It compares standard SAEs, including the SAE Bench suite, with Matryoshka SAEs. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that Matryoshka SAEs reduce absorption and splitting and improve concept isolation at a slight reconstruction cost. They argue scaling pathologies are artifacts of myopic training objectives, not fundamental limitations.
record.recipe_differences: Uses nested reconstruction objectives at multiple dictionary prefixes rather than the standard single-dictionary SAE objective; compares against standard SAE architectures.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature absorption and related quality outcomes vary with SAE objective and loss weighting; the weighted Matryoshka ablation performs worse on absorption than equal weighting.

fits_no_version.finding: Average maximum decoder cosine similarity is lower for Matryoshka SAEs (Fig. 8). Meta-SAEs explain 55% of BatchTopK vs 42% of Matryoshka decoder variance (App. D.1). The study reads both as less feature composition.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard sparsity objectives produce composed latents with shared decoder structure that grows with dictionary size.

record.problems: The cross-size TinyStories evidence is qualitative and uses selected examples. The paper says its tree visualizations are targeted rather than comprehensive, and multi-parent relationships are simplified for display. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the reported absorption and splitting results.
record.rows_left_out: No other results in the text directly measure the claim's feature splitting, absorption, or cross-size feature relations.

untested.parts: Whether child latents jointly cover the parent's inputs and whether their decoder directions lie near the parent direction. The cross-size trees use activation similarity only.
Comparison against the one-layer setting; open-release coverage is only via the SAE Bench suite on Gemma-2-2B layer 12.
Entire version: no test of geometrically close nested families mirroring a model hierarchy.
Whether changing dictionary size or sparsity alone within standard SAEs fails to fix absorption is not captured in the rows; Figures 6 and 10 may bear on it.
Entire version: no test of larger latents decomposing into smaller-SAE latents or of novel latents. Leask et al. is only cited.

missing.what: Absorption and splitting rates across all six SAE Bench architectures and L0 = 20 to 320. Only L0=40 BatchTopK vs Matryoshka is recorded; needed to check whether sparsity changes fix absorption.
Scaling evaluation at 4k, 16k and 65k dictionary sizes, including absorption. The text says Matryoshka improves or stays stable while other architectures often degrade.
Stop-gradient ablation (better absorption at low L0) and group-count ablation (3 groups worse absorption, 10 groups slightly better).
General statement that reference SAEs of 30 to 10k latents across three locations show smaller SAEs with broad concepts that larger SAEs fragment.

record.verdict_notes: T2 rather than T5. The study is not an original source for any version. V2 evidence comes from SAE Bench baseline SAEs on Gemma-2-2B; TinyStories is a 4-layer model, not a large one. The TinyStories evidence is qualitative and drawn from selected examples. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures splitting and gives qualitative cross-size examples, but does not establish that child features jointly partition the coarse feature's inputs or measure their decoder-direction proximity.
Tests TinyStories and Gemma-2-2B, but not open SAE releases or the full range of large models and SAE families.
The cross-size tree method uses activation similarity; the study does not test nested families of geometrically close decoder directions that mirror a model hierarchy.
The study shows absorption and a Matryoshka intervention that reduces it, but does not isolate whether changing dictionary size or sparsity alone fixes absorption.
Does not test whether larger latents decompose into combinations of smaller latents or whether larger dictionaries add novel latents.
Tests nested reconstruction objectives against standard SAE training and a weighted variant; it does not test Matryoshka SAEs as a general solution across all objectives or input structures.

rows.subject: Vanilla SAE (toy model)
rows.operation_detail: Trained a standard SAE on a synthetic hierarchical-feature dataset.

conditions.value: tree-structured binary features; child features only appear with their parent

rows.measure: Whether the parent latent activates when child features are active
rows.value: The parent latent does not activate when one of its child features is active.
rows.note: The paper describes this as feature absorption.
rows.check: None; the vanilla toy parent latent fails to fire when a child fires.

source_check.locator_found: Sec 4.1, Fig 3; App C.1 (20 latents, ReLU)

rows.subject: Matryoshka SAE (toy model)
rows.operation_detail: Trained an SAE with nested reconstruction objectives on a synthetic hierarchical-feature dataset.

conditions.value: tree-structured binary features; child features only appear with their parent

rows.measure: Whether the parent latent activates when child features are active
rows.baseline: Vanilla SAE: parent does not activate when a child feature is active
rows.value: Parent features remain active regardless of which child features are active.
rows.note: The paper says the Matryoshka SAE recovers the underlying feature structure.
rows.check: For V4 the absorption effect is absent under Matryoshka. For V6 this is the predicted objective-driven removal, so V6 reads as observed. A row has one state, so absent is recorded relative to V4.

rows.subject: Vanilla SAE (toy model)
rows.operation_detail: Compared learned decoder vectors with ground-truth feature vectors using cosine similarity.
rows.measure: Cosine similarity between learned latent decoder vectors and ground-truth feature vectors
rows.value: High similarity between parent and child latents; the paper describes redundant representations and failure to disentangle hierarchical features.
rows.note: No numerical cosine values are given in the text.
rows.check: None; qualitative heatmap with no numbers.

rows.subject: Matryoshka SAE (toy model)
rows.operation_detail: Compared learned decoder vectors with ground-truth feature vectors using cosine similarity.
rows.measure: Cosine similarity between learned latent decoder vectors and ground-truth feature vectors
rows.baseline: Vanilla SAE: high similarity between parent and child latents
rows.value: A clear diagonal similarity structure, with minimal overlap and only small nonzero off-diagonal terms.
rows.note: The paper interprets this as recovery of the true feature vectors.
rows.check: None; qualitative heatmap with no numbers.

rows.subject: 4-layer TinyStories Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Compared reference SAEs of different dictionary sizes and traced related latents across them.
rows.measure: Cross-size relationship and activation coverage of a general female-words latent
rows.baseline: S/2/65 in the 300-latent SAE fires on “she,” “her,” “girl,” and female names including “Lily” and “Sue.”
rows.value: In the 1000-latent SAE, S/3/66 stops firing on “Lily”; the paper attributes this hole to the specialized Lily latent S/3/359 absorbing that case.
rows.note: A qualitative example of cross-size feature absorption; the paper does not report whether the related latents' decoder directions are nearby.
rows.check: State should be observed: the text reports a clear hole and a specialized Lily latent splitting off as the dictionary grows from 300 to 1000. V2 removed: a 4-layer TinyStories model is neither a large model nor an open SAE release. The cross-size link uses activation-based masked cosine similarity, not decoder proximity.

rows.subject: 4-layer TinyStories Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Trained a 25k-latent Matryoshka SAE and examined coverage of female-coded tokens and specialized latents.

conditions.value: same average sparsity as the comparison described in the text

rows.measure: Coverage of the general feature alongside specialized child features
rows.baseline: The 1000-latent reference SAE has a Lily-related hole in its general female-words feature.
rows.value: Maintains broad coverage of female-coded tokens while developing specialized Sue, Lily, and female-names latents without holes.
rows.check: A single Matryoshka SAE, not a dictionary-size progression, so V1 and V2 are removed. For V4 absorption is absent (no holes). For V6 this is the predicted objective effect.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Used first-letter classification probes to measure when SAE latents fail to activate on tokens starting with a letter and are absorbed into token-aligned latents.
rows.note: The text reports this as the comparison at average sparsity L0 of 40.
rows.check: V1 removed: an absorption rate at a single dictionary size does not show splitting as size grows. The baseline field should read 'not stated' rather than the Matryoshka value. The 0.05 vs 0.49 comparison is at L0=40.

source_check.problem: The baseline is the study's own Matryoshka value of 0.05. It is a comparison, not a true baseline, but the cell is right.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Used first-letter classification probes to measure absorption into token-aligned latents.
rows.note: The paper describes the Matryoshka rate as significantly reduced, not eliminated.
rows.check: V1 and V2 removed: this is the study's own method, not the version's standard-SAE pattern. Against V4, absorption is strongly reduced but not zero (0.05). For V6 the reduction is as predicted.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured how many latents are needed to capture first-letter features.
rows.measure: Number of latents needed per first-letter feature
rows.baseline: Matryoshka SAE: one latent per first letter on average
rows.value: BatchTopK SAE: information split across three latents.
rows.note: The text does not state whether the three latents jointly partition the same input set or have nearby decoder directions.
rows.check: V1 removed: a single size, not a growth progression. It shows first-letter information split over about three latents in a standard BatchTopK SAE on Gemma-2-2B.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured how many latents are needed to capture first-letter features.
rows.measure: Number of latents needed per first-letter feature
rows.baseline: BatchTopK SAE: information split across three latents
rows.value: Matryoshka SAE: one latent per first letter on average.
rows.note: This is a count of latents, not a direct test of whether their inputs partition or their directions are close.
rows.check: V1 and V2 removed: this is the study's own Matryoshka method, which reduces splitting to about one latent per letter.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Trained a Weighted Matryoshka variant with losses weighted by the number of new latents in each group.
rows.measure: Feature absorption and spurious correlation removal
rows.value: The weighted variant performs worse on feature absorption and spurious correlation removal metrics.
rows.note: The paper reports the direction of the difference but gives no numeric absorption value in the text.
rows.check: The weighted variant is worse on absorption than equal-weight Matryoshka, so the reduction depends on loss weighting. No numbers are given in the text.

source_check.notes: Same-group work (2 shared authors with an original). TinyStories evidence is one selected qualitative example. Not in rows (figure only): Fig 6 (six SAE Bench architectures), Fig 10 (4k/16k/65k), App G.2/G.3 ablations. The study introduces Matryoshka SAEs, which V6 names; confirm it is not a V6 original.

statements.correction: This text: reference SAEs of 30, 100, 300, 1k, 3k and 10k latents on attention outputs, MLP outputs and the residual stream. The location of the S series is not named. S/2/65 (300 latents) fires on she, her, girl, Lily and Sue. S/3/66 (1000 latents) stops firing on Lily, which S/3/359 absorbs. S/3/861 is a Sue latent.
statements.problem: The condition 'layer 3 pre-attention residual (post)' is not in this text. It may come from the lw post, but the merged conditions line applies it to both. The rest of what it says about this study is right.
The text confirms only a qualitative TinyStories example. The counts can't be checked here.

statements.correction: Absorption 0.49 (BatchTopK) vs 0.05 (Matryoshka) and three vs one latent per first letter: layer 12, 65536, L0=40. Fig 10: dictionary sizes 4k, 16k and 65k, averaged over L0 40/80/160. The text says alternative architectures often degrade with scale. No values in text.
